interactions.mechanism: St. John's wort induces P-gp and CYP3A pathways that can lower direct oral anticoagulant exposure. Lower exposure can reduce protection against stroke or venous thromboembolism.
interactions.management: Avoid St. John's wort with apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban unless the prescriber explicitly manages the interaction. Do not start or stop St. John's wort without notifying the anticoagulant prescriber.
interactions.evidence_notes: DailyMed labeling for apixaban and rivaroxaban explicitly names St. John's wort among combined P-gp/CYP3A inducers to avoid; dabigatran and edoxaban labels warn against P-gp inducers that reduce exposure.

interactions.mechanism: Potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes add to the potassium-retaining effect of potassium-sparing diuretics, increasing risk of severe hyperkalemia and arrhythmia.
interactions.management: Avoid potassium supplements and potassium salt substitutes with spironolactone, eplerenone, finerenone, amiloride, or triamterene unless specifically prescribed with serum potassium monitoring.
interactions.evidence_notes: Spironolactone labeling warns against potassium supplementation and high-potassium salt substitutes because of hyperkalemia risk.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's wort can induce P-glycoprotein activity and reduce digoxin exposure. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic range, so reduced concentrations can compromise heart failure or atrial fibrillation control.
interactions.management: Avoid adding St. John's wort to digoxin therapy without prescriber oversight. If unavoidable, monitor serum digoxin concentration and clinical response when St. John's wort is started or stopped.
interactions.evidence_notes: Human pharmacokinetic evidence and digoxin labeling support a clinically relevant reduction in digoxin concentration with St. John's wort.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium can chelate tetracycline-class antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk.
interactions.management: Separate calcium supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Iron can chelate tetracycline-class antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk.
interactions.management: Separate iron supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Magnesium can chelate tetracycline-class antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk.
interactions.management: Separate magnesium supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Zinc can chelate tetracycline-class antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk.
interactions.management: Separate zinc supplements from doxycycline, tetracycline, and related antibiotics by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: Green tea catechins, especially EGCG, can inhibit intestinal uptake transporters and markedly reduce nadolol exposure. Human studies report reduced nadolol plasma exposure and reduced blood-pressure effect.
interactions.management: Avoid concentrated green tea extract with nadolol. For brewed green tea, consult the prescriber about timing and blood pressure monitoring rather than assuming separation fully prevents the interaction.
interactions.evidence_notes: Human pharmacokinetic studies show substantial nadolol exposure reduction with green tea or EGCG-concentrated green tea extract.

interactions.mechanism: Iron can chelate fluoroquinolone antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk during an active infection.
interactions.management: Separate iron supplements from ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and related fluoroquinolones by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.
interactions.evidence_notes: Current ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin DailyMed labels instruct separation from iron-containing products because absorption is reduced.

interactions.mechanism: Magnesium can chelate fluoroquinolone antibiotics in the gut, reducing antibiotic absorption and increasing treatment-failure risk during an active infection.
interactions.management: Separate magnesium supplements or magnesium-containing antacids from ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, and related fluoroquinolones by the interval specified on the antibiotic label or by the prescriber.
interactions.evidence_notes: Current ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin DailyMed labels instruct separation from magnesium-containing products because absorption is reduced.

interactions.mechanism: Vitamin K is required to activate clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X. Warfarin reduces vitamin K activity. A sudden increase in vitamin K intake can reduce the anticoagulant effect; a sudden decrease can increase it.
interactions.management: This is a consistency warning, not a ban. Keep vitamin K intake from food and supplements about the same each day. Tell your prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting, stopping, or changing any supplement containing vitamin K; INR monitoring may be needed after a change. Do not change warfarin on your own.
interactions.evidence_notes: Vitamin K directly antagonizes warfarin mechanism. This is stated on every warfarin drug label. NIH ODS Vitamin K fact sheet explicitly warns anticoagulant users.

interactions.mechanism: Omega-3 fatty acids (EPA/DHA) inhibit platelet aggregation and thromboxane A2 synthesis, adding antiplatelet activity on top of warfarin's anticoagulant effect. High doses (≥3 g/day) can meaningfully increase bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Use fish oil supplements cautiously with warfarin. Doses up to 1 g/day are generally low risk. Inform your doctor; monitor for bruising or unusual bleeding. INR monitoring is advisable when starting or stopping high-dose fish oil.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: fish oil up to 1 g/day is low-risk with warfarin; >1 g warrants INR monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgo inhibits platelet-activating factor (PAF) and has antiplatelet activity independent of warfarin's mechanism. The combination significantly amplifies bleeding risk. Case reports of serious hemorrhagic events exist.
interactions.management: Avoid combining ginkgo with warfarin. If ginkgo is being used, inform prescriber immediately. Watch for signs of bleeding (unusual bruising, prolonged cuts, blood in urine/stool).
interactions.evidence_notes: Mixed: observational data suggest increased bleeding risk, but controlled studies at recommended doses show no significant effect. Severity reflects precautionary approach for anticoagulant users.

interactions.mechanism: Garlic (Allium sativum) inhibits platelet aggregation via ajoene and other sulfur compounds. Combined with warfarin, it increases antiplatelet burden and may elevate bleeding risk. Some evidence of mild CYP2C9 inhibition.
interactions.management: Use garlic supplements cautiously with warfarin. Culinary amounts are generally safe. High-dose garlic supplements (>600 mg/day) warrant INR monitoring. Report any unusual bruising.
interactions.evidence_notes: Mainly case reports. Culinary amounts are safe. Concentrated supplements may have mild antiplatelet effect.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused garlic bleeding floor (600 mg); pair mgmt agrees (>600 mg supplement); culinary safe.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort (Hypericum perforatum) is a potent inducer of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. It significantly accelerates warfarin metabolism, reducing plasma concentrations and anticoagulant effect. INR can fall to sub-therapeutic levels, increasing thrombosis risk.
interactions.management: Do not use St. John's Wort while taking warfarin. INR must be monitored closely if it is started or stopped. Switching to a different antidepressant approach is strongly recommended.

interactions.mechanism: Vitamin E can inhibit platelet aggregation and antagonize vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. NIH notes that large supplemental doses may increase bleeding risk with warfarin, but the amount needed for a clinically significant effect is uncertain.
interactions.management: Contains vitamin E. Large supplemental doses may increase bleeding risk with warfarin, but the amount that causes a clinically significant effect is uncertain. Tell your prescriber or anticoagulation clinic before starting, stopping, or changing this supplement, and keep your use consistent — extra monitoring may be appropriate after a change. Do not change warfarin on your own. This alert reflects the presence of vitamin E; it does not mean a known dose limit was crossed.

interactions.mechanism: CoQ10 is structurally similar to vitamin K2 and may exert a mild pro-coagulant effect, potentially reducing warfarin's efficacy. Case reports describe decreased INR when CoQ10 is added to warfarin therapy.
interactions.management: Monitor INR if starting CoQ10 while on warfarin. Dose adjustments may be needed. Inform your prescriber.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor and uncertain INR signal; retain as background context without gating product fit.
interactions.mechanism: Case reports suggest glucosamine (alone or with chondroitin) may increase INR in warfarin users. The mechanism is not well established; possible mild CYP2C9 inhibition or direct effect on coagulation cascade.
interactions.management: Monitor INR when starting glucosamine. Report any unusual bruising or bleeding. Effect may be small but warrants awareness.

interactions.mechanism: Cranberry juice and extracts may inhibit CYP2C9, the primary enzyme responsible for warfarin (S-enantiomer) metabolism. This can elevate warfarin levels and INR. Case reports include fatal hemorrhage.
interactions.management: Limit cranberry consumption to small amounts (occasional serving of juice/food). Avoid large quantities of cranberry juice or concentrated supplements. Monitor INR closely if intake changes.

interactions.mechanism: Curcumin inhibits platelet aggregation and thromboxane formation. At supplement doses (500–2000 mg/day), it may add antiplatelet activity on top of warfarin's anticoagulant effect, increasing bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Culinary turmeric is generally safe. High-dose curcumin supplements warrant INR monitoring. Inform prescriber before starting curcumin supplements.

dose_threshold.rationale: High-dose curcumin (>500 mg/day, per the sibling anticoagulant pair) with warfarin; culinary turmeric safe.

interactions.mechanism: Dong quai (Angelica sinensis) contains coumarin derivatives with intrinsic anticoagulant properties, and may also inhibit platelet aggregation. Combined with warfarin, it can substantially increase INR and bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Avoid dong quai while taking warfarin. INR should be checked if the herb was recently used. Inform prescriber.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor dose-dependent bleeding signal; culinary and lower supplemental exposure should not gate product fit.
interactions.mechanism: Ginger (Zingiber officinale) has mild antiplatelet properties via thromboxane synthase inhibition. At culinary doses the effect is negligible; high-dose supplements may add to warfarin's antiplatelet burden.
interactions.management: Culinary ginger is safe. High-dose ginger supplements (>2 g/day) warrant awareness. Report unusual bruising. INR monitoring is reasonable if high-dose ginger is started.
interactions.evidence_notes: Theoretical based on in-vitro platelet inhibition. Clinical evidence for interaction at dietary doses is weak.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: high-dose ginger supplements (>2 g/day) with warfarin; culinary ginger safe.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, significantly increasing statin metabolism (especially simvastatin, atorvastatin, lovastatin). Plasma statin levels fall by up to 50%, substantially reducing cardiovascular protection.
interactions.management: Do not use St. John's Wort with CYP3A4-metabolized statins. If herbal antidepressant therapy is desired, discuss alternatives with your doctor. Monitor for reduced lipid-lowering effect if combined inadvertently.

verification.notes: Wave 6.Y Batch 9.A. PMID 17701167 (Andren 2007) is the direct human PK study of SJW + atorvastatin; 31742659 is the updated clinical-relevance review; 15260917 is the pharmacokinetic-interactions mechanism review. All three content-verified via PubMed efetch 2026-05-27; titles+abstracts directly support the CYP3A4/P-gp induction → reduced statin exposure mechanism the entry describes.

interactions.mechanism: Red yeast rice naturally contains monacolin K, which is chemically identical to lovastatin. Combining red yeast rice with a prescription statin doubles the effective statin dose, dramatically increasing risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis.
interactions.management: Do not use red yeast rice if you are already taking a prescription statin. If you prefer a natural approach, discuss with your doctor — the two should not be combined. Seek immediate care for severe muscle pain, weakness, or dark urine.

verification.notes: Wave 6.Y Batch 9.A. PMIDs content-verified via PubMed efetch 2026-05-27. 36779111 is a direct case report of RYR-induced rhabdomyolysis; 40909457 documents severe RYR-induced rhabdomyolysis with AKI + respiratory failure (severity tail justifying Major); 33538260 is the JACC focus seminar on RYR for hypercholesterolemia documenting the monacolin K = lovastatin equivalence the mechanism text relies on. Official NCCIH + FDA sources retained as primary regulatory anchor.

interactions.mechanism: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit irreversibly inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, increasing bioavailability of CYP3A4-metabolized statins (simvastatin, atorvastatin, lovastatin). This raises statin plasma levels and muscle toxicity risk.
interactions.management: Simvastatin labeling says to avoid grapefruit juice. Lovastatin labeling warns that grapefruit juice raises lovastatin levels and myopathy risk. Atorvastatin labeling advises against large quantities (more than 1.2 liters a day). Pravastatin, rosuvastatin, and fluvastatin are not significantly affected. Spacing simvastatin or lovastatin from grapefruit juice can reduce but does not remove the effect. Spacing atorvastatin does not reliably reduce the effect. Dose spacing is not a substitute for the label precautions above.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Grapefruit and grapefruit juice can raise blood levels of some statins by slowing an enzyme in the gut that breaks them down. The effect is large with simvastatin and lovastatin; with atorvastatin it matters mainly with large amounts of juice (more than 1.2 liters a day). Higher statin levels can raise the chance of muscle aches or weakness.
interactions.practical_guidance: On simvastatin, skip grapefruit juice. On lovastatin, ask your prescriber before having grapefruit. On atorvastatin, avoid large amounts (more than 1.2 liters a day). Pravastatin, rosuvastatin and fluvastatin aren't affected by grapefruit.

interactions.mechanism: High-dose niacin (≥1 g/day, pharmacologic dose) combined with statins increases risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. The mechanism is additive muscle toxicity, possibly related to impaired CoQ10 synthesis and mitochondrial dysfunction.
interactions.management: Pharmacologic niacin doses require physician supervision when combined with statins. Monitor for muscle pain, weakness, or brown urine. Nutritional niacin doses from multivitamins are generally safe.

verification.notes: Wave 6.Y Batch 9.A. PMIDs content-verified via PubMed efetch 2026-05-27. 22085343 is AIM-HIGH (Boden 2011 NEJM), the landmark RCT showing no incremental CV benefit of niacin added to intensive statin therapy plus the adverse-event signal. 25014686 is HPS2-THRIVE primary outcomes (Landray 2014 NEJM), the largest niacin+statin trial documenting the myopathy and hepatotoxicity signal. 23444397 is the HPS2-THRIVE design + pre-specified muscle and liver outcomes paper documenting the elevated myopathy/hepatic-event rates that anchor the 'monitor for muscle pain, weakness, or brown urine' management text. High-dose niacin qualifier (≥1 g/day pharmacologic dose) intentionally retained to avoid generic multivitamin B3 warnings.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pharmacologic niacin (>=1 g/day) drives statin-myopathy risk; nutritional/multivitamin niacin doses are safe.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort (hypericin, hyperforin) inhibits reuptake of serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine. Combined with SSRIs, this creates severe serotonergic excess leading to serotonin syndrome: agitation, hyperthermia, clonus, seizures, and potentially death.
interactions.management: Never combine St. John's Wort with any SSRI, SNRI, or other serotonergic agent. A washout period equivalent to 5 half-lives of the SSRI is required before switching. Seek emergency care immediately if serotonin syndrome symptoms appear.

interactions.mechanism: 5-HTP (5-hydroxytryptophan) is the direct precursor to serotonin. Taking 5-HTP while on an SSRI floods the serotonin system from both the supply side (increased synthesis) and the reuptake side (blocked clearance), creating a high risk of serotonin syndrome.
interactions.management: Avoid 5-HTP while taking any SSRI. If transitioning from an SSRI to 5-HTP for mood support, a full washout of the SSRI is required. Consult your doctor before using 5-HTP.

interactions.mechanism: SAMe is involved in monoamine metabolism and has antidepressant properties partly via serotonergic mechanisms. Combined with SSRIs, it can cause additive serotonergic stimulation. Case reports of serotonin syndrome exist.
interactions.management: Avoid combining SAMe with SSRIs without medical supervision. If used as an adjunct (some practitioners do this), requires careful dose titration and monitoring for agitation, tremor, or hyperthermia.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgo has antiplatelet activity; SSRIs also impair platelet function by depleting serotonin in platelets. Combined, bleeding risk is increased. Additionally, ginkgo may have serotonin-modulating properties that could interact with SSRIs.
interactions.management: Avoid high-dose ginkgo with SSRIs. If used for cognitive support, discuss with your doctor. Monitor for unusual bruising.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused ginkgo antiplatelet floor (120 mg, standard EGb-761 dose).

interactions.background_rationale: Drug-specific sedation monitoring signal; keep visible as background context without a categorical product verdict.
interactions.mechanism: Fluvoxamine strongly inhibits CYP1A2, the main enzyme metabolizing melatonin. Fluvoxamine with melatonin can substantially increase melatonin exposure and cause excessive sedation.
interactions.management: Ask the fluvoxamine prescriber before using melatonin. If the combination is approved, use only the dose they recommend and monitor for excessive drowsiness; do not drive or operate machinery if impaired.

interactions.mechanism: ACE inhibitors reduce aldosterone secretion, causing potassium retention. Additional potassium supplementation can lead to dangerous hyperkalemia (elevated serum potassium), causing cardiac arrhythmias and potentially cardiac arrest.
interactions.management: Do not take potassium supplements while on ACE inhibitors without medical supervision. Avoid potassium-based salt substitutes. Regular serum potassium monitoring is essential if any potassium supplementation is used.

interactions.mechanism: Glycyrrhizin in licorice root inhibits 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, leading to mineralocorticoid excess, sodium retention, potassium loss, and elevated blood pressure. This directly opposes antihypertensive therapy.
interactions.management: Avoid licorice root supplements (glycyrrhizin-containing) while on antihypertensives. DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) is safer. Blood pressure should be re-checked if licorice exposure is suspected.

interactions.mechanism: Ephedra (ephedrine alkaloids) stimulates alpha and beta adrenergic receptors, raising heart rate and blood pressure. Beta blockers block beta receptors, leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, causing paradoxical hypertension. Combined cardiac effects are unpredictable.
interactions.management: Do not use ephedra or products containing ephedrine alkaloids with beta blockers. Note: Ephedra was banned for dietary supplements in the US in 2004 but persists in some herbal products marketed outside the US.

interactions.mechanism: Furanocoumarins in grapefruit inhibit intestinal CYP3A4, increasing plasma levels of CYP3A4-metabolized calcium channel blockers (felodipine, nifedipine, amlodipine). Elevated CCB levels can cause excessive blood pressure lowering, dizziness, and reflex tachycardia.
interactions.management: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice with CYP3A4-metabolized calcium channel blockers. Effects can last 24–72 hours after consuming grapefruit. Check with your pharmacist about your specific CCB.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Grapefruit slows down how your body processes some blood pressure medicines (felodipine, nifedipine, amlodipine), so more of the drug ends up in your bloodstream. This can cause dizziness, flushing, or low blood pressure.
interactions.practical_guidance: Skip grapefruit and grapefruit juice while on these medicines. The effect can last 1–3 days, so timing the dose around grapefruit doesn't really help.

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence modest blood-pressure effect; informational monitoring only.
interactions.mechanism: CoQ10 has been shown in some trials to modestly lower blood pressure (~10–17 mmHg systolic). When combined with antihypertensive medications, this additive effect is usually beneficial, but can occasionally cause excessive blood pressure reduction.
interactions.management: CoQ10 can be a useful adjunct in hypertension management. Monitor blood pressure when starting CoQ10. Dose adjustment of antihypertensives may be needed in some cases.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED floor at the supplemental CoQ10 dose (~100 mg) where a modest BP effect is reported; trace amounts below.

interactions.mechanism: Alpha-lipoic acid (ALA) improves insulin sensitivity and glucose uptake. Combined with metformin or other diabetes medications, it can cause additive blood glucose lowering, potentially resulting in hypoglycemia.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose when adding ALA to diabetes therapy. Dose adjustments may be needed. Common in integrative diabetes care but requires tracking glucose responses.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused ALA glucose floor (600 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Chromium might lower blood glucose. With insulin or other diabetes medications, the additive effect could increase the risk of low blood glucose.
interactions.management: Chromium may lower blood glucose, which may add to your diabetes medication's effect. Monitor your glucose more closely when starting or changing chromium, and ask the clinician managing your diabetes whether any monitoring or medication change is needed — do not change medication on your own. Shown when the supplemental total is at least 200 mcg/day: a screening threshold inferred from studied dose ranges, not a proven toxicity cutoff or guideline cutoff.
interactions.background_rationale: Potential additive glucose lowering supports monitoring, not a categorical product-level caution.

dose_threshold.rationale: Authored screening floor inferred from studied supplemental dose ranges; 200 mcg/day is not a guideline cutoff or proven toxicity threshold.

interactions.mechanism: Berberine activates AMPK, closely mimicking metformin's mechanism of action. Clinical trials show HbA1c reductions comparable to metformin. Combined use can cause significant hypoglycemia. Berberine also inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2D6, affecting metabolism of multiple drugs.
interactions.management: Berberine should not be combined with diabetes medications without physician supervision. Frequent blood glucose monitoring is essential. Dose adjustments are commonly required.

interactions.mechanism: Bitter melon (Momordica charantia) contains charantin and polypeptide-p, which have insulin-like activity and stimulate glucose uptake. Combined with diabetes medications, additive hypoglycemia can occur.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose when using bitter melon with diabetes medications. Dose adjustment may be needed. Do not use as a replacement for prescribed therapy.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused bitter melon glucose floor (600 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Fenugreek seeds contain soluble fiber and compounds that slow carbohydrate absorption and may enhance insulin secretion, causing additive glucose lowering when combined with diabetes medications.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose when using fenugreek supplements with diabetes medications. Dose adjustment may be needed. Inform your prescriber.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused fenugreek glucose floor (500 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Gymnema sylvestre may stimulate insulin secretion and improve beta-cell function. Combined with secretagogues or insulin, it can cause additive hypoglycemia.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose carefully. Inform your prescriber. Dose adjustments to diabetes medications may be required.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused gymnema glucose floor (400 mg).

interactions.background_rationale: Minor dose-dependent glucose signal; culinary exposure is outside the alert layer.
interactions.mechanism: Cinnamon extracts have modest insulin-sensitizing properties. At supplemental doses it may produce mild additional glucose lowering, especially with secretagogues.
interactions.management: Culinary cinnamon is safe. High-dose cinnamon supplements with diabetes medications warrant glucose monitoring. Note: Cassia cinnamon (most common) contains coumarin, which can be harmful in large amounts.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused cinnamon glucose floor (500 mg extract); culinary cinnamon safe.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium forms insoluble complexes with levothyroxine in the GI tract, reducing its absorption by about 20–25% when taken together. This can result in inadequately controlled hypothyroidism.
interactions.management: Take levothyroxine at least 4 hours before or after calcium supplements. Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 30–60 minutes before breakfast. Monitor thyroid function tests if supplementation regimen changes.

interactions.mechanism: Ferrous sulfate and other iron supplements form insoluble complexes with levothyroxine in the GI tract, reducing levothyroxine absorption significantly. This is a well-documented interaction affecting thyroid control.
interactions.management: Take levothyroxine at least 4 hours before or after iron supplements. Monitor TSH levels after starting or stopping iron. Women often take both and need to manage this timing carefully.

interactions.mechanism: Magnesium can bind levothyroxine in the GI tract and reduce its absorption. In a 2025 crossover trial, magnesium aspartate lowered levothyroxine absorption by 12% and magnesium citrate by 7% (not significant), a smaller effect than reported for calcium or iron.
interactions.management: Take magnesium supplements at least 4 hours away from levothyroxine. Morning levothyroxine with evening magnesium is a practical approach.

interactions.mechanism: Soy isoflavones and soy protein can impair levothyroxine absorption and may also affect thyroid hormone metabolism. The effect is most pronounced in infants but relevant at high supplemental doses in adults.
interactions.management: Separate levothyroxine from soy-rich foods or supplements by at least 4 hours. Patients with hypothyroidism on stable levothyroxine should have TSH re-checked if starting high-dose soy isoflavone supplements.

verification.notes: PMID 16571087 (Messina & Redmond, Thyroid 2006) content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27 — title matches the soy-thyroid interaction claim. Replaces prior empty source_pmids that violated critical_no_hallucinated_citations.

interactions.mechanism: Coffee, particularly espresso, can reduce levothyroxine absorption when taken simultaneously. Polyphenols and other coffee compounds may interfere with GI absorption.
interactions.management: Take levothyroxine with water only, at least 30–60 minutes before coffee. This is a standard clinical recommendation for all thyroid patients.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Coffee, especially espresso, can reduce how much levothyroxine your body absorbs when you take them close together. This isn't dangerous, but it can mean your thyroid medicine doesn't work as well.
interactions.practical_guidance: Take levothyroxine with water on an empty stomach, and wait at least 30–60 minutes before having coffee or breakfast.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort is a potent CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inducer. Cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and sirolimus — all transplant immunosuppressants — are CYP3A4/P-gp substrates. Concomitant use can reduce drug levels by 50–70%, leading to acute transplant rejection.
interactions.management: Absolutely contraindicated in transplant patients. Do not use St. John's Wort with any calcineurin inhibitor or mTOR inhibitor. Emergency INR/drug level monitoring is required if accidental exposure occurred.

interactions.mechanism: Echinacea is an immune stimulant. In transplant recipients or patients on immunosuppressants for autoimmune disease, immune stimulation can overcome the intended immunosuppression, triggering organ rejection or disease flare.
interactions.management: Avoid echinacea with any immunosuppressant therapy. Transplant patients and those on immunosuppressants for autoimmune conditions should not use echinacea for colds or immune support.

interactions.mechanism: Cat's claw (Uncaria tomentosa) has immunostimulant properties that may oppose immunosuppressive therapy, potentially reducing drug efficacy in transplant or autoimmune patients.
interactions.management: Avoid cat's claw with immunosuppressants. Inform prescriber of all herbal supplements being taken.

interactions.mechanism: Astragalus (Astragalus membranaceus) has documented immunomodulatory effects, including upregulation of T-cell and NK cell activity. This may counteract immunosuppressive drugs in transplant or autoimmune patients.
interactions.management: Avoid astragalus with immunosuppressant therapy. Discuss all herbal supplements with your transplant or rheumatology team.

interactions.mechanism: Grapefruit inhibits CYP3A4, increasing blood levels of cyclosporine, tacrolimus, and sirolimus. Elevated immunosuppressant levels increase toxicity risk (nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, infection risk).
interactions.management: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice with transplant immunosuppressants. Maintain consistent dietary patterns; avoid sudden changes in grapefruit intake.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.note_body: Grapefruit raises the level of transplant medicines (cyclosporine, tacrolimus, sirolimus) in your blood. Even small changes in level matter for these drugs because they have a narrow safe range.
interactions.practical_guidance: Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice entirely while on transplant immunosuppressants. Be consistent — even occasional grapefruit can shift your levels.

interactions.mechanism: Long-term phenytoin therapy can lower folate status. Folate supplementation can lower serum phenytoin concentrations in some people, potentially affecting seizure control.
interactions.management: If you take phenytoin, discuss folate intake and any supplement dose with the prescribing clinician. Do not start high-dose folic acid on your own; phenytoin levels or seizure control may need monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Gamma-linolenic acid (GLA) in evening primrose oil has been reported to lower the seizure threshold. In patients with epilepsy on anticonvulsants, this can precipitate breakthrough seizures.
interactions.management: Avoid evening primrose oil in patients with epilepsy or on anticonvulsant therapy. Use alternative omega-6 sources if needed.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgotoxin (4'-O-methylpyridoxine) in ginkgo seeds and some leaf preparations can lower seizure threshold. Additionally, ginkgo may induce CYP2C19, potentially reducing valproate levels.
interactions.management: Use ginkgo with caution in patients with seizure history. Seizure monitoring is recommended. High-quality, standardized ginkgo leaf extract with controlled ginkgotoxin levels is preferable.

interactions.mechanism: MAO-A in the intestinal wall normally breaks down dietary tyramine. When MAO is inhibited, tyramine is absorbed intact and releases massive norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals, causing a hypertensive crisis: severe headache, blood pressure spikes to dangerous levels, stroke, and death.
interactions.management: Strict low-tyramine diet is mandatory with MAOIs. Avoid: aged cheeses, cured meats, fermented foods, tap beer, overripe fruit, soy sauce, miso, tofu, and fava beans. Work with a dietitian. Carry a hypertensive crisis emergency plan.

verification.notes: Food advisory note; PMIDs content-verified via PubMed esummary on 2026-05-27.

interactions.evidence_notes: MAOI + tyramine hypertensive crisis is one of the most established drug-food interactions in clinical pharmacology. FDA black box warning on all MAOI labels.
interactions.note_body: MAOIs block an enzyme that normally breaks down tyramine in foods like aged cheese, cured meats, fermented foods, and tap beer. With the enzyme blocked, tyramine can spike blood pressure quickly.
interactions.practical_guidance: A low-tyramine diet is essential while on MAOIs. Your prescriber or a dietitian should walk you through the food list. Headache, sweating, or chest pain after a meal can mean a tyramine reaction — call your prescriber.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort inhibits serotonin, dopamine, and norepinephrine reuptake. Combined with an MAOI, which prevents monoamine degradation, the resulting monoamine excess causes severe serotonin syndrome and potentially fatal hypertensive crisis.
interactions.management: Absolutely contraindicated. St. John's Wort must not be used with any MAOI. A 14-day washout after stopping an MAOI is required before any serotonergic supplement.
interactions.evidence_notes: St Johns Wort is a known serotonergic agent. Combination with MAOIs carries serotonin syndrome risk. NCCIH and FDA both warn against this combination.

interactions.mechanism: 5-HTP is the immediate serotonin precursor. With MAO inhibited, 5-HTP-derived serotonin cannot be degraded, causing catastrophic serotonin accumulation and serotonin syndrome.
interactions.management: Never combine 5-HTP with an MAOI. Do not start 5-HTP after stopping an MAOI until the prescriber confirms the product-specific washout interval has been completed.
interactions.evidence_notes: 5-HTP is a direct serotonin precursor. Combination with MAOIs is universally contraindicated due to serotonin syndrome risk. Clinical pharmacology consensus.

interactions.mechanism: SAMe has serotonergic activity and monoamine-modulating properties. Combined with an MAOI, it can potentiate serotonin syndrome risk through additive serotonergic load.
interactions.management: Contraindicated. Do not use SAMe with any MAOI. Observe appropriate washout periods.
interactions.evidence_notes: SAMe has documented serotonergic activity. NCCIH explicitly warns against combination with serotonergic drugs including MAOIs.

interactions.mechanism: Ginseng has stimulant and sympathomimetic-like properties. With MAO inhibited, the catecholaminergic activity of ginseng can contribute to hypertensive reactions and CNS overstimulation.
interactions.management: Avoid ginseng with MAOIs. Case reports of hypomania and headache with this combination exist. Use ginseng only after full MAOI washout.

interactions.mechanism: NSAIDs reduce platelet thromboxane A2 synthesis and GI mucosal protection. Omega-3s additionally inhibit platelet aggregation. Combined, GI bleeding risk and systemic antiplatelet effect are additive.
interactions.management: Use caution combining high-dose fish oil (>2 g/day) with NSAIDs. Take NSAIDs with food to protect GI lining. Monitor for GI symptoms. Discuss with doctor if using regularly.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: caution combining fish oil >2 g/day with NSAIDs; lower doses low-risk.

interactions.mechanism: Garlic supplements have antiplatelet activity via inhibition of arachidonic acid and thromboxane pathways. Combined with NSAIDs (which also inhibit COX-dependent platelet activation), bleeding risk is additive.
interactions.management: Avoid high-dose garlic supplements with regular NSAID use. Culinary garlic is generally safe. Watch for unusual bruising or GI bleeding.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused garlic bleeding floor; culinary garlic safe with NSAIDs.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgo inhibits PAF and platelet aggregation. NSAIDs inhibit COX-mediated thromboxane synthesis. The combined antiplatelet effect increases GI and systemic bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Avoid ginkgo with regular NSAID use. Watch for GI bleeding, unusual bruising. Inform prescriber of all supplements.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused ginkgo antiplatelet floor (120 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Willow bark contains salicin, which is metabolized to salicylate (aspirin-like compound). Combining willow bark with NSAIDs or aspirin creates additive salicylate toxicity and GI mucosal damage risk.
interactions.management: Do not combine willow bark supplements with NSAIDs or aspirin. This combination is essentially double-dosing salicylate drugs. Seek medical advice for pain management if both are considered.

interactions.mechanism: Valerian has GABAergic activity and CNS sedative properties. Combined with sedative medications (including benzodiazepines, sleep aids, antihistamines), it produces additive CNS depression, excessive sedation, and impaired psychomotor function.
interactions.management: Avoid valerian with prescription sedatives or sleep medications. Do not drive or operate machinery if using both. Inform your doctor.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor at a sedative valerian-root dose (~400 mg; typical 300-600 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Kava (Piper methysticum) has CNS depressant and kavalactone-mediated GABAergic activity. Combined with sedatives or benzodiazepines, it causes additive sedation and respiratory depression. Kava also has hepatotoxic potential that may be enhanced by other CNS drugs.
interactions.management: Do not combine kava with sedatives, benzodiazepines, or alcohol. Kava alone carries hepatotoxicity warnings. Combined use amplifies both CNS and liver risks.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor additive drowsiness signal; background counseling rather than a product-fit gate.
interactions.mechanism: Melatonin has mild sedative properties. Combined with benzodiazepines, it may produce additive drowsiness. The interaction is generally mild and melatonin is sometimes used therapeutically to help patients taper benzodiazepines.
interactions.management: Use low-dose melatonin (0.5–3 mg) with benzodiazepines if needed for sleep. Avoid activities requiring alertness. Inform your doctor.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: low-dose melatonin (0.5-3 mg) is fine with benzodiazepines; floor at 5 mg (above the sleep-dose range).

interactions.mechanism: Passionflower (Passiflora incarnata) has GABAergic sedative activity. Combined with sedatives, benzodiazepines, or hypnotics, it can produce additive CNS depression.
interactions.management: Avoid passionflower with sedative medications. Do not drive after combining. Use under physician guidance.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor at a sedative passionflower dose (~400 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Glycyrrhizin inhibits 11-beta-HSD2, which normally inactivates cortisol in peripheral tissues. Combined with corticosteroids, this increases the effective glucocorticoid activity and exacerbates potassium loss, fluid retention, and hypertension.
interactions.management: Avoid licorice root supplements with corticosteroid therapy. Monitor blood pressure and potassium. DGL licorice has reduced glycyrrhizin and is safer.

interactions.mechanism: Echinacea stimulates immune function including cytokine production. Corticosteroids are used to suppress immune responses. These opposing mechanisms may reduce therapeutic efficacy of corticosteroids.
interactions.management: Avoid echinacea with corticosteroid therapy for immune suppression (transplant, autoimmune). For short-course corticosteroids (allergies, asthma exacerbation), the interaction is less critical but still worth noting.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, accelerating the metabolism of estrogen and progestin components of oral contraceptives. This reduces OC plasma levels and may cause contraceptive failure, leading to unintended pregnancy.
interactions.management: Do not use St. John's Wort with oral contraceptives. Use a backup contraceptive method if concurrent use occurred. Discuss with your prescriber regarding timing before resuming reliance on OC alone.

interactions.mechanism: Chasteberry (Vitex agnus-castus) acts on dopamine receptors to reduce prolactin and may modulate progesterone and LH secretion. This hormonal activity may interfere with oral contraceptives' progestin-mediated effects.
interactions.management: Avoid chasteberry with hormonal contraceptives. The interaction is theoretical but relevant given chasteberry's hormonal activity. Inform your OB/GYN.

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence high-dose isoflavone signal; dietary soy should not produce an alert.
interactions.mechanism: Soy isoflavones (genistein, daidzein) are phytoestrogens that bind estrogen receptors. They may weakly compete with or add to the estrogenic component of OCs. Clinical significance at typical dietary intake is minimal.
interactions.management: Dietary soy is generally safe with OCs. High-dose soy isoflavone supplements (>100 mg/day) warrant caution. Discuss with your prescriber.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: high-dose soy isoflavone supplements (>100 mg/day) warrant caution; dietary soy safe with OCs.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium competitively inhibits iron absorption in the small intestine by competing for DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1) and potentially forming insoluble complexes. Both heme and non-heme iron absorption are reduced when taken simultaneously with calcium.
interactions.management: Take iron and calcium supplements at different times — at least 2 hours apart. Iron is best absorbed on an empty stomach in the morning. Calcium can be taken with meals or at bedtime.

interactions.mechanism: Catechins and tannins in green tea bind non-heme iron, forming insoluble iron-polyphenol complexes that cannot be absorbed. This can reduce iron absorption by 50–90% when consumed together.
interactions.management: Do not take iron supplements with green tea extract or green tea beverages. Separate by at least 2 hours. Take iron with vitamin C instead to enhance absorption.

interactions.mechanism: High zinc intake induces intestinal metallothionein, a protein that binds copper tightly. Copper bound to metallothionein is not released into circulation and is lost when intestinal cells slough off. Chronic high-dose zinc (>40 mg/day) causes copper deficiency.
interactions.management: PharmaGuide displays this review when the known zinc total is at least 25 mg/day. This is a conservative screening threshold, not a proven toxicity cutoff. Long-term higher-dose zinc can reduce copper status; ask a clinician whether copper monitoring or a balanced formulation is appropriate.

dose_threshold.rationale: Conservative review floor for prolonged supplemental zinc use; this is not a toxicity cutoff.

interactions.mechanism: St. John's Wort inhibits serotonin reuptake. 5-HTP increases serotonin synthesis as a direct precursor. Combined, these supplements produce additive serotonin loading, potentially causing serotonin syndrome even without prescription medications.
interactions.management: Do not combine St. John's Wort with 5-HTP. Choose one or the other for mood support. If either is used with prescription serotonergic drugs, additional caution is required.

interactions.mechanism: 5-HTP increases serotonin synthesis as a direct precursor. SAMe is involved in monoamine neurotransmitter metabolism and may interact with supplements that increase serotonin. Combining them can add serotonergic load and increase serotonin-syndrome risk.
interactions.management: Avoid combining 5-HTP with SAMe unless a clinician is deliberately supervising serotonergic supplement use. Watch for agitation, tremor, diarrhea, fever, sweating, or confusion if they were taken together.
interactions.evidence_notes: MSK and NCCIH describe serotonin-risk concerns for 5-HTP/SAMe and advise avoiding multiple serotonin-affecting supplements; direct pair evidence is limited, so this remains a precautionary Major stack warning.

interactions.mechanism: Kava is metabolized hepatically and can inhibit CYP2E1, the enzyme responsible for converting acetaminophen to the hepatotoxic metabolite NAPQI. However, both kava and high-dose acetaminophen are hepatotoxic — combined use substantially increases risk of liver damage.
interactions.management: Avoid kava with regular acetaminophen use. If pain relief is needed, use the lowest effective dose of acetaminophen and avoid alcohol. Monitor liver enzymes with long-term exposure.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor possible additive blood-pressure effect; monitor in the background only.
interactions.mechanism: Magnesium has mild calcium channel blocking and vasodilatory properties. High-dose supplementation can modestly lower blood pressure, adding to antihypertensive drug effects.
interactions.management: Magnesium is generally safe with antihypertensives. Monitor blood pressure when starting magnesium. Beneficial in patients with hypomagnesemia or metabolic syndrome.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED floor at the supplemental-magnesium UL (350 mg); dietary magnesium below is not a meaningful BP modifier.

interactions.background_rationale: Minor additive drowsiness signal; background counseling rather than a product-fit gate.
interactions.mechanism: Some antipsychotics (olanzapine, clozapine) are metabolized by CYP1A2 and also cause sedation. Melatonin can add mild sedative effect and fluvoxamine (sometimes used with antipsychotics) can raise melatonin levels significantly.
interactions.management: Use low-dose melatonin (0.5–3 mg) if needed for sleep with antipsychotics. Monitor for excessive sedation. Inform your psychiatrist.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: low-dose melatonin (0.5-3 mg) is fine with antipsychotics; floor at 5 mg.

interactions.mechanism: CBD inhibits CYP2C9 and CYP3A4, the primary enzymes metabolizing warfarin and other anticoagulants. This can substantially increase anticoagulant blood levels, elevating INR and bleeding risk. The FDA-approved CBD drug (Epidiolex) carries this interaction warning.
interactions.management: Monitor INR closely if CBD is started or stopped with warfarin. Dose adjustment of warfarin may be required. Inform prescriber of all CBD use including oils and capsules.

interactions.mechanism: CBD inhibits CYP3A4 and CYP2C9, affecting metabolism of many antihypertensive drugs (amlodipine, losartan, others). Elevated drug levels can cause excessive blood pressure reduction, dizziness, or syncope.
interactions.management: Inform prescriber of CBD use with blood pressure medications. Monitor blood pressure when starting or stopping CBD. CBD dose and drug dose may both need adjustment.

interactions.mechanism: CBD inhibits CYP3A4 and OATP1B1/1B3 transporters, both of which are involved in statin metabolism. This can raise statin plasma concentrations, increasing risk of myopathy and hepatotoxicity.
interactions.management: Inform prescriber of CBD use with statin therapy. Monitor for muscle pain, weakness, or elevated liver enzymes. Dose adjustment may be needed.

interactions.mechanism: Vinpocetine inhibited P-glycoprotein in vitro; the clinical relevance is uncertain. CYP inhibition occurred above expected human exposures, making a clinical CYP interaction unlikely (PMID 28930203). A small study in 18 healthy men found only a minute warfarin effect, considered unlikely to have clinical implications (PMID 2272713). These findings do not establish clinically important potentiation across the anticoagulant class; this warning is precautionary.
interactions.management: Avoid starting vinpocetine while taking warfarin or another anticoagulant unless your prescriber is managing the combination. If you already take both, tell your anticoagulation clinician and ask whether additional monitoring is needed.

verification.approval_provenance: Prior approval confirmed by the project owner on 2026-09-11; no new clinician review represented.
verification.review_note: Retained Moderate severity and precautionary class scope. Evidence remains theoretical with low confidence; the cited studies do not establish clinically important class-wide potentiation.

interactions.mechanism: Health Canada lists horse chestnut among natural health products with evidence that they may change warfarin levels or directly affect blood clotting. Horse chestnut seed extracts contain aescin/escin and are used for venous insufficiency, so anticoagulant users need bleeding-risk monitoring rather than a silent clean check.
interactions.management: Use caution with horse chestnut seed extract while taking warfarin or another anticoagulant. Tell the anticoagulation clinician before adding or stopping it, keep intake consistent if already using it, and watch for unusual bruising or bleeding.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor at standardized horse-chestnut-seed (aescin) supplement dose (~300 mg); not a guideline cutoff.

interactions.mechanism: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) has been shown in clinical trials to reduce fasting blood glucose and HbA1c. Combined with diabetes medications, it can cause additive glucose lowering.
interactions.management: Monitor blood glucose when adding ashwagandha to diabetes therapy. Inform prescriber. Dose adjustment may be needed.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor at a standardized ashwagandha-extract dose (~300 mg); not a guideline cutoff.

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence possible blood-pressure effect; informational monitoring only.
interactions.mechanism: Ashwagandha has mild adaptogenic blood pressure-lowering effects in some studies. Combined with antihypertensives, minor additive effects are possible.
interactions.management: Monitor blood pressure when starting ashwagandha with antihypertensive therapy. Generally well-tolerated but inform prescriber.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor at a standardized ashwagandha-extract dose (~300 mg).

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence additive sedation signal; background counseling rather than a categorical warning.
interactions.mechanism: Ashwagandha has anxiolytic and mild sedative properties via GABAergic mechanisms. Combined with sedative medications, it may add to CNS depressant effects.
interactions.management: Use caution combining ashwagandha with sedatives. Avoid driving or operating machinery if drowsiness occurs. Inform prescriber.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor at a standardized ashwagandha-extract dose (~300 mg).

interactions.mechanism: Curcumin inhibits platelet aggregation via multiple pathways (COX inhibition, TXA2 suppression, cAMP elevation). With anticoagulant/antiplatelet drugs, this produces additive bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Use caution with high-dose curcumin supplements (>500 mg/day) with anticoagulants. Culinary turmeric is generally safe. Monitor for unusual bruising or bleeding.

dose_threshold.rationale: Pair mgmt: curcumin >500 mg/day with anticoagulants; culinary turmeric safe.

interactions.mechanism: HIV protease inhibitors (indinavir, ritonavir, saquinavir, etc.) are CYP3A4/P-gp substrates. St. John's Wort induces both, causing a 50–80% reduction in protease inhibitor plasma levels, leading to virological failure and drug resistance.
interactions.management: Absolutely contraindicated. St. John's Wort must not be used with any antiretroviral therapy. This interaction has led to treatment failures and HIV drug resistance. The FDA has issued specific warnings.

interactions.mechanism: In severely immunocompromised patients, live probiotic bacteria (particularly Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium) carry a risk of bacteremia or sepsis (rare but reported). The risk is greatest with Saccharomyces boulardii (fungemia risk) in immunocompromised hosts.
interactions.management: Avoid probiotics containing live organisms in severely immunocompromised patients (transplant, chemotherapy). Discuss with transplant or oncology team. Heat-killed probiotics or postbiotics are safer alternatives.

interactions.mechanism: Panax ginseng may reduce the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. A controlled trial found ginseng reduced warfarin AUC and INR. The mechanism may involve CYP induction or direct procoagulant ginsenoside effects.
interactions.management: Monitor INR closely if taking ginseng with warfarin. INR may need to be checked more frequently and warfarin dose adjusted.

interactions.background_rationale: Low-confidence modest blood-pressure signal; informational monitoring only.
interactions.mechanism: Vitamin D deficiency is associated with renin-angiotensin system activation and elevated blood pressure. Correction of deficiency may modestly lower blood pressure, potentially adding to antihypertensive effects.
interactions.management: Vitamin D supplementation is generally recommended for deficient patients on antihypertensives. Monitor blood pressure when correcting significant deficiency. Usually beneficial rather than problematic.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED floor at the adult UL (4000 IU); repletion doses below are usually beneficial rather than additive-hypotensive.

interactions.mechanism: Both omega-3 fatty acids and vitamin E suppress platelet aggregation via separate pathways (membrane phospholipid remodeling and inhibition of platelet thromboxane synthesis), producing additive antiplatelet effects.
interactions.management: Monitor for signs of easy bruising or bleeding. Consider keeping supplemental vitamin E below high-dose ranges (≤400 IU/day, roughly 180-268 mg alpha-tocopherol depending on form) when taking fish oil.

dose_threshold.rationale: Reused vitamin E bleeding floor (400 IU/day) normalized to a conservative 180 mg alpha-tocopherol equivalent. NIH ODS lists 1 IU synthetic vitamin E as 0.45 mg alpha-tocopherol and 1 IU natural vitamin E as 0.67 mg; 180 mg is the lower mass equivalent, so below this floor is below 400 IU for either form.

interactions.mechanism: Both omega-3 fatty acids and ginkgo biloba (via ginkgolides inhibiting PAF) independently inhibit platelet aggregation, producing additive antiplatelet/bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Monitor for signs of bruising or prolonged bleeding, especially before surgery. Consider separating or reducing doses.

dose_threshold.rationale: Sup-Sup additive bleeding; floor on ginkgo (primary antiplatelet, 120 mg standard dose).

interactions.background_rationale: Minor dose-dependent additive drowsiness signal; background counseling only.
interactions.mechanism: Valerian acts as a GABAergic/adenosine modulator promoting sleep, while melatonin acts on MT1/MT2 receptors; combined use produces additive CNS sedation and may increase next-day drowsiness.
interactions.management: Start with lower doses of both if combining. Avoid driving or operating machinery after taking both.

dose_threshold.rationale: INFERRED conservative floor on valerian (~400 mg) for additive sedation with melatonin.

interactions.mechanism: Divalent cations (Mg2+, Ca2+) form insoluble chelate complexes with bisphosphonate molecules in the GI tract, severely reducing oral bioavailability.
interactions.management: Take bisphosphonates on an empty stomach with plain water. Wait at least 30-60 minutes before any mineral supplements.

interactions.mechanism: Ginkgolides (particularly ginkgolide B) are potent PAF antagonists; concurrent use with aspirin (COX-1) or clopidogrel (P2Y12) produces additive inhibition of platelet activation, increasing bleeding risk.
interactions.management: Avoid combining ginkgo with antiplatelet drugs. Discontinue ginkgo at least 7 days before surgery.

interactions.mechanism: Calcium ions can form poorly absorbed complexes with oral ciprofloxacin, reducing ciprofloxacin exposure and risking antibiotic treatment failure.
interactions.management: Take oral ciprofloxacin at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium-containing supplements, multivitamins, or antacids, as directed by the prescription label.

interactions.mechanism: Zinc can bind oral fluoroquinolones in the gastrointestinal tract, reducing antibiotic absorption and risking treatment failure.
interactions.management: Separate oral fluoroquinolones from zinc-containing supplements and multivitamins. The timing interval differs by drug, so follow the prescription label or pharmacist instructions; do not apply one interval to the entire class.

interactions.mechanism: MAOIs irreversibly inhibit monoamine oxidase, preventing serotonin breakdown. SSRIs block serotonin reuptake. Combined serotonergic load causes rapid serotonin accumulation, triggering life-threatening serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, seizures, cardiovascular collapse).
interactions.management: Never combine. A 14-day washout after stopping an MAOI is required before starting any SSRI. After stopping fluoxetine, 5 weeks are needed before starting an MAOI due to its long half-life.

interactions.mechanism: Meperidine (pethidine) inhibits serotonin reuptake in addition to opioid receptor activity. Combined with MAOIs, this causes an excitatory serotonin syndrome reaction: hyperthermia, rigidity, seizures, and potentially fatal cardiovascular instability.
interactions.management: Absolutely contraindicated. Meperidine must never be used in patients on MAOIs or within 14 days of stopping them. Use morphine or other opioids that lack serotonergic activity if analgesia is required.

interactions.mechanism: MAOIs block the breakdown of norepinephrine and dopamine, so adding a sympathomimetic stimulant (amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, methylphenidate) can trigger a hypertensive crisis — a sudden, severe, potentially fatal rise in blood pressure, with risk of stroke, heart attack, or seizure. FDA labels for amphetamine- and methylphenidate-family stimulants, and for the MAOIs phenelzine and tranylcypromine, explicitly contraindicate co-use with an MAOI or within 14 days of stopping one.
interactions.management: Do not take an MAOI and a stimulant together. Allow at least 14 days between stopping an MAOI and starting a stimulant, and the same when switching the other way. If you are taking both, contact the prescriber managing your MAOI right away.

verification.notes: DailyMed label check confirmed the Adderall XR label published May 06, 2026 and methylphenidate extended-release tablet label published Jun 24, 2026, both from the DailyMed database published Jun 26, 2026.

interactions.evidence_notes: Promoted from Major/avoid to Contraindicated on 2026-06-27: FDA labels for amphetamine, lisdexamfetamine, and methylphenidate products, and for the MAOIs phenelzine (Nardil) and tranylcypromine (Parnate), explicitly contraindicate or prohibit MAOI co-use (hypertensive-crisis risk, 14-day washout). The one class exception is selegiline — oral low-dose and transdermal (Emsam) labels say 'monitor blood pressure' rather than contraindicate — which warrants a selegiline-specific carve-out once the interaction engine supports most-specific-wins precedence. Until then the safe class default is Contraindicated, because over-warning rare selegiline use is preferable to under-warning the common, label-contraindicated amphetamine/methylphenidate pairs (under-warning is the bigger clinical risk).

interactions.mechanism: Both methotrexate and trimethoprim inhibit dihydrofolate reductase, depleting intracellular folate. Combined inhibition causes severe, additive bone marrow suppression — pancytopenia, megaloblastic anemia, and mucositis — that can be fatal.
interactions.management: Avoid this combination. If anti-infective therapy is required in a patient on methotrexate, use an alternative antibiotic that does not inhibit folate metabolism (e.g., amoxicillin). If inadvertent exposure occurs, monitor CBC and initiate leucovorin rescue.

interactions.mechanism: Erythromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. Ergotamine is a CYP3A4 substrate with a narrow therapeutic index. CYP3A4 inhibition raises ergotamine plasma levels dramatically, causing severe vasospasm, peripheral ischemia, and potentially irreversible tissue necrosis.
interactions.management: Contraindicated. Do not use erythromycin (or any potent CYP3A4 inhibitor: clarithromycin, ritonavir, itraconazole) in patients using ergotamine-containing migraine medications. Use a macrolide with lower CYP3A4 inhibition (azithromycin) if an antibiotic is needed.

interactions.mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit platelet COX-1 and erode gastric mucosa, increasing GI bleeding risk. When combined with anticoagulants (warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban), the additive effect on hemostasis sharply elevates risk of serious or fatal GI hemorrhage. Some NSAIDs also displace warfarin from albumin, transiently raising free drug levels.
interactions.management: Avoid chronic NSAID use with anticoagulants. If short-term NSAID use is unavoidable, use the lowest effective dose, add a PPI for gastric protection, and monitor closely for signs of bleeding.

interactions.mechanism: ACE inhibitors reduce angiotensin II-mediated aldosterone secretion, decreasing renal sodium reabsorption. The sodium deficit triggers compensatory proximal tubular sodium and lithium retention, raising serum lithium levels into the toxic range (>1.5 mEq/L).
interactions.management: If the combination is unavoidable, check serum lithium within 5–7 days of starting the ACE inhibitor and after any dose change. Maintain adequate sodium intake. Watch for early lithium toxicity signs: tremor, nausea, ataxia, confusion.

interactions.mechanism: Thiazide diuretics cause renal sodium wasting. Sodium depletion triggers compensatory proximal tubular reabsorption of both sodium and lithium, dramatically increasing serum lithium concentration and risk of toxicity.
interactions.management: Avoid thiazide diuretics in patients on lithium if possible. If required, reduce lithium dose empirically, increase monitoring frequency (lithium level within 5–7 days), and ensure adequate sodium and fluid intake.
interactions.evidence_notes: Thiazide diuretics reduce lithium clearance, causing accumulation and toxicity. This interaction is stated on lithium drug labels and is a standard pharmacology teaching point.

interactions.mechanism: Simvastatin is a CYP3A4 substrate. Erythromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor that can raise simvastatin AUC up to 6-fold. Elevated simvastatin levels increase risk of myopathy and life-threatening rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury.
interactions.management: Avoid combining erythromycin with simvastatin or lovastatin. Temporarily suspend the statin if short-course erythromycin is needed. Alternative statins with lower CYP3A4 dependence (pravastatin, rosuvastatin) carry lower interaction risk.

interactions.mechanism: Both ondansetron and fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, ciprofloxacin, moxifloxacin) independently block cardiac hERG potassium channels, prolonging the QT interval. Additive QT prolongation raises the risk of torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death, especially in patients with electrolyte abnormalities or underlying cardiac disease.
interactions.management: Avoid co-administration when possible. If both are clinically necessary, obtain a baseline ECG, correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia before starting, and monitor ECG during treatment. Use the lowest effective dose of each.

interactions.mechanism: Spironolactone (potassium-sparing diuretic) blocks aldosterone and reduces urinary potassium excretion. ACE inhibitors also reduce aldosterone levels via the renin-angiotensin system. Combined, both agents retain potassium independently, producing additive hyperkalemia — which can cause fatal cardiac arrhythmias.
interactions.management: Use this combination with caution only when clinically indicated (e.g., heart failure post-RALES). Monitor serum potassium and creatinine closely — within 1 week of starting and after any dose change. Avoid potassium supplements and potassium-containing salt substitutes.

interactions.mechanism: SSRIs increase synaptic serotonin via reuptake inhibition. Triptans are serotonin 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists. Combined serotonergic activity can precipitate serotonin syndrome (agitation, hyperreflexia, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), though the absolute risk is debated.
interactions.management: The FDA issued an alert (2006) on this combination. Use the lowest effective triptan dose if both are needed. Counsel patients on serotonin syndrome warning signs and seek immediate care for rapid-onset agitation, muscle twitching, fever, or rapid heart rate.

interactions.mechanism: Iodinated contrast agents can acutely impair renal function (contrast-induced nephropathy). Metformin is renally cleared; acute kidney injury causes metformin accumulation, blocking hepatic lactate metabolism and producing potentially fatal lactic acidosis. Note: this is a procedural drug-drug interaction, not a chronic DDI.
interactions.management: Hold metformin at the time of or before any procedure using IV iodinated contrast. Restart only after renal function is confirmed stable — typically 48 hours post-procedure. Patients with pre-existing renal impairment require closer monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires CYP2C19 activation to its active antiplatelet metabolite. Omeprazole (and esomeprazole) are potent CYP2C19 inhibitors. Co-administration reduces clopidogrel active metabolite exposure by up to 45%, diminishing platelet inhibition and potentially increasing cardiovascular event risk in high-risk patients (post-ACS, post-stent).
interactions.management: Avoid omeprazole and esomeprazole with clopidogrel. If a PPI is needed for gastric protection, use pantoprazole or rabeprazole, which have minimal CYP2C19 inhibitory activity.

interactions.mechanism: Fluconazole is a potent inhibitor of CYP2C9 and moderate inhibitor of CYP3A4. Most statins (simvastatin, lovastatin, atorvastatin) depend on CYP3A4; fluvastatin and rosuvastatin depend on CYP2C9. CYP inhibition raises statin AUC substantially, increasing myopathy and rhabdomyolysis risk.
interactions.management: Avoid combining fluconazole with simvastatin, lovastatin, or fluvastatin. If antifungal azole therapy is required, temporarily suspend the statin or switch to pravastatin (CYP-independent). Resume statin after completing the fluconazole course.

interactions.mechanism: Beta blockers reduce heart rate and AV conduction via beta-1 blockade. Verapamil (non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker) independently slows SA and AV node conduction. Combined, additive negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects can produce severe bradycardia, heart block, or asystole — particularly with IV administration.
interactions.management: Use together only when clinically necessary with careful monitoring. Avoid IV verapamil in patients on beta blockers. Monitor heart rate and ECG at initiation and dose changes. Dose reductions of one or both agents may be required.

interactions.mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4, reducing renal and non-renal digoxin clearance. Digoxin plasma levels can rise 70–100% within days of starting amiodarone, pushing into the toxic range (>2 ng/mL). Digoxin toxicity causes bradycardia, heart block, and potentially fatal arrhythmias.
interactions.management: Reduce the digoxin dose by 30–50% when starting amiodarone. Monitor digoxin levels closely within 1 week and again after 1 month. Maintain levels in the 0.5–0.9 ng/mL therapeutic range for heart failure.

interactions.mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the primary enzyme responsible for theophylline metabolism. CYP1A2 inhibition can double theophylline plasma levels, causing theophylline toxicity: nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, seizures.
interactions.management: If ciprofloxacin is required in a patient on theophylline, reduce theophylline dose by 30–50% and monitor serum theophylline levels. Use an alternative antibiotic when possible (azithromycin has minimal CYP1A2 inhibition).

interactions.mechanism: Acetaminophen at higher doses (>2 g/day regularly) inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis via an unclear mechanism, potentiating warfarin's anticoagulant effect and raising INR. The interaction is dose-dependent — occasional low-dose use has minimal impact.
interactions.management: Acetaminophen at ≤2 g/day is the preferred analgesic over NSAIDs for patients on anticoagulants. At higher or chronic doses, monitor INR more frequently. Advise patients to report any signs of unusual bruising or bleeding.

interactions.mechanism: Enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, oxcarbazepine, topiramate) upregulate CYP3A4 and conjugation enzymes, markedly accelerating metabolism of ethinyl estradiol and progestins in combined oral contraceptives. The result is reduced OC plasma levels and failure to suppress ovulation — unintended pregnancy.
interactions.management: Counsel patients on the interaction. Consider higher-dose OC formulations, additional barrier contraception, or switch to a non-hormonal or long-acting reversible contraceptive (IUD, implant) that is not affected by enzyme induction.

interactions.mechanism: A complex bidirectional interaction: valproic acid displaces phenytoin from protein binding (raising free phenytoin transiently) and inhibits CYP2C9-mediated phenytoin metabolism (raising total phenytoin). Simultaneously, phenytoin induces valproate metabolism, lowering valproate levels. Net effect is unpredictable changes in both drug levels, risking toxicity or loss of seizure control.
interactions.management: Monitor both free phenytoin and valproate levels when used together. Dose adjustments for both agents are typically required. Neurologist oversight is essential. Avoid initiating both simultaneously — introduce one at a time with careful level monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: Corticosteroids impair gastric mucosal defense by reducing prostaglandin synthesis and mucus production. NSAIDs further inhibit COX-1-dependent mucosal protection. Combined, the risk of gastric and duodenal ulcers, GI bleeding, and perforation increases approximately 15-fold compared to either agent alone.
interactions.management: Add a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) when corticosteroids and NSAIDs must be used together. Minimize duration and dose of NSAIDs. Consider switching to acetaminophen for analgesia when anti-inflammatory effect is not required.

interactions.mechanism: Antipsychotics cause CNS and respiratory depression. Benzodiazepines enhance GABA-A inhibition, producing sedation and respiratory suppression. Combined, additive CNS depression can cause excessive sedation, respiratory depression, aspiration, and death. clozapine and IV lorazepam have been specifically associated with fatal cardiorespiratory collapse.
interactions.management: Avoid parenteral combination. For oral use, use the lowest necessary doses of both agents, monitor respiratory status, and avoid in patients with sleep apnea or compromised respiratory reserve. Alert patients and caregivers to signs of excessive sedation.

interactions.mechanism: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin stores (by blocking serotonin reuptake transporter SERT on platelets), impairing platelet aggregation. NSAIDs further impair platelet function via COX-1 inhibition and cause GI mucosal erosion. Combined use raises the risk of upper GI bleeding 3–15 fold compared to either drug alone.
interactions.management: Add a PPI when SSRIs and NSAIDs are co-prescribed, particularly in patients over 65 or with prior GI bleeding. Consider acetaminophen as an alternative analgesic for patients on SSRIs.

interactions.mechanism: Alcohol inhibits gluconeogenesis and increases lactate production by shifting NAD+/NADH ratio. Metformin also reduces hepatic lactate clearance. Heavy or binge alcohol intake combined with metformin increases lactic acidosis risk, especially in patients with hepatic impairment, renal insufficiency, or dehydration. Note: this is a lifestyle drug interaction.
interactions.management: Advise patients on metformin to avoid heavy or binge drinking. Moderate alcohol consumption (1–2 standard drinks/occasion) is generally acceptable in the absence of hepatic or renal impairment. Reinforce hydration, especially during illness.

interactions.mechanism: Loop and thiazide diuretics cause renal potassium and magnesium wasting. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia both increase myocardial sensitivity to digoxin's toxic effects at any given serum level — AV block, ventricular arrhythmias, and even therapeutic levels become toxic when electrolytes are depleted.
interactions.management: Monitor serum potassium and magnesium regularly in patients on digoxin plus loop or thiazide diuretics. Replace electrolytes promptly. Consider potassium-sparing strategies. Target potassium >4.0 mEq/L in digoxin-treated patients.

interactions.mechanism: Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1 hepatic uptake transporter, dramatically increasing plasma concentrations of many statins (especially simvastatin, cerivastatin, rosuvastatin). Elevated statin levels substantially increase the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis. This combination caused cerivastatin's market withdrawal in 2001.
interactions.management: Avoid gemfibrozil with most statins. If combined lipid-lowering therapy is required, fenofibrate has significantly lower interaction potential. If gemfibrozil is necessary, use pravastatin at the lowest effective dose with vigilant myopathy monitoring.

interactions.mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandin synthesis, causing sodium and water retention and vasoconstriction. This blunts the blood pressure-lowering effect of most antihypertensive drug classes (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, beta blockers, diuretics, CCBs). Blood pressure can rise significantly, even with occasional NSAID use.
interactions.management: Avoid chronic NSAID use in patients with hypertension. For analgesic needs, acetaminophen is preferred. If NSAIDs are used short-term, monitor blood pressure closely and counsel patients to track home readings.

interactions.mechanism: Benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-A-mediated CNS depression. Opioids cause mu-receptor-mediated respiratory depression independent of GABAergic pathways. Combined, the two mechanisms act synergistically — not merely additively — to suppress respiratory drive, causing profound hypoventilation, hypoxia, and death. FDA issued a Black Box Warning in 2016 for this combination.
interactions.management: Avoid concurrent prescribing. When both are medically necessary, use the lowest effective dose of each, limit duration, monitor respiratory status closely, and prescribe naloxone to patients and caregivers. Never take with alcohol. Counsel patients on the combination's lethality.

interactions.mechanism: Cholestyramine can bind concomitant oral medicines in the gut and delay or reduce the absorption of warfarin. Starting, stopping, or changing the timing of cholestyramine can therefore change warfarin exposure and anticoagulant control.
interactions.management: Take warfarin at least 1 hour before or 4 to 6 hours after cholestyramine unless the anticoagulation clinician gives different instructions. Keep the timing consistent and contact the warfarin prescriber or anticoagulation service when starting, stopping, or changing cholestyramine; INR monitoring may be needed. Do not change warfarin on your own.

verification.notes: RxNorm live properties verified RxCUI 2447 as cholestyramine resin and RxCUI 11289 as warfarin. DailyMed explicitly names warfarin and gives the asymmetric oral-drug timing interval.

interactions.evidence_notes: Current DailyMed cholestyramine labeling states that cholestyramine may delay or reduce warfarin absorption and directs other oral drugs at least one hour before or four to six hours after cholestyramine.
